question: Is a wali (guardian) required for a valid Islamic marriage?
answer:
For today's Q&A, we're going to have a lengthy discussion answering a number of questions that I've gotten over the last few months regarding the necessity of having a wali during the marriage or the nikah ceremony. In other words, what are the various opinions about the necessity of having a guardian, a wali, for the marriage to be considered valid? And what is to be done if there is a clash between the bride and the wali, and there doesn't seem to be an agreement on that issue?

Now, this question actually is very sensitive. A few weeks ago I had given a response to another question, and I simply mentioned in passing that the majority opinion is that a wali is required, and then I moved on. After that lecture I got dozens of emails from around the world, generally speaking positive, but quite a few were very long emails explaining that I should be more careful in what I say. They didn't agree with this position. They said that one of the schools of law allows the woman to get married without the wali, the issues of updating Islamic fiqh, this and that.

So all of these questions... And of course, one of the largest genres of questions that any scholar in the West gets is with regards to marriage and divorce. And this is one of those issues of marriage: what is one to do when two people want to get married — the bride and the groom, or the fiancé — they know they want to get married, and the wali becomes involved, and the wali says, "I'm not wanting this marriage to take place. I'm not happy in this particular instance. I don't want this particular groom. I have something else in mind for you." And of course, this is the standard clash that we hear about all the time. We've all gone through that phase of our lives, those of us that are beyond that phase.

And so it is important for us to take a critical look at what Islamic law says, look at the reality, and see what can be done. Before I begin: this is going to be a lengthy lecture. It's not just the evidences, because we really do have to take a step back. We have to understand that this is an issue of importance to many young men and especially young women. This is a very, very common theme, and it is one of the largest sources of conflict, really, of a young lady's life. She might be going to college or just entering the workforce, and she meets somebody she wants to marry. They get along very well, they think that they're perfect for one another, and then for whatever reason the wali objects. And then of course the whole drama ensues, which is the standard back and forth between her and the wali and other family members. And the issue comes: why can't she make this decision, when she can make decisions with regards to other aspects of her life?

And therefore we do need to take a step back and understand that we as Muslims do have a very different philosophy of the conception of family, and yes, even of gender. The role and the notion of family and of gender is something that is relatively fluid in the Western context. By fluid we mean it changes; it keeps on morphing from one understanding to another. And from our perspective, it is the Shari'ah that defines the role of the family and the role of the gender. At times, our values from our Shari'ah are not fully in consonance and agreement with the values of our society around us.

And we have to be very clear in this regard: what is to be done when our laws seem to conflict with the values that we've absorbed from our society? Because what we've absorbed, really, is the sense of individualism. What we've absorbed is the sense of: it's my life, it's my pleasure, it's the rest of my life, why should I take into account what my parents say? I'm not saying everything we absorb from the world around us, from the society around us, is necessarily evil. But we do need to be cognizant of the fact that, okay, the Shari'ah does allow for change. So is this something we can change or not, with regards to our modern times?

And before I even get into the evidences of fiqh, we also have to discuss just a little bit the philosophy of the 'ulama, of the scholars themselves, when it comes to how much we take modern society into account. Because as you're probably aware, for so many issues there's going to be a spectrum of opinion, and the answer that you get will depend on the scholar that you ask. For many issues of Islamic law — and this is no exception — when it comes to the issue of the wali, you will find a classical difference of opinion. And then of course in our modern times, you will find even more people debating this issue.

Within the spectrum, within this gamut of scholarship, obviously there are some scholars who feel that we should not take anything of modernity and of cultural differences into account. We should simply stick with the tradition: whatever our books have taught us, whatever the fiqh that they studied was, they should simply copy and paste, and they should ignore the world around them. Because they feel, from their paradigm, that the job of the Shari'ah is not to conform to society; rather, society should conform to the Shari'ah. So they have their paradigm.

Then you have, of course, the flip, opposite side of the spectrum: those who feel that we look at what they call the goals of the Shari'ah, the maqasid al-Shari'ah, and they will always find a mechanism or a way to bring their understanding of the Shari'ah into harmony with the modern understanding of the world. These are the people that are typically on the more modernist or the progressive side of the spectrum, and within themselves they also have quite a lot of differences.

Now obviously you're asking me, or you're listening to my lecture right now, so obviously I should just put my cards on the table. I've said this many times, and if you listen to my lectures and my Q&As you know exactly where I am coming from: in the grand scale of things, I do consider myself to be, for lack of a better label, a forward-thinking traditionalist. By this I mean that we understand that we come from a tradition. We cannot just discard the tradition. We understand that our Shari'ah, our fiqh, our laws have been built over the last 14 centuries. We understand that there is a human element, no doubt about that, but we also understand that there is a divine component as well. Not everything is subjective.

We have to be very careful that we don't enter this Pandora's box of ultimate post-modernism. We have to be very careful that we don't just accept the notion that there is no ultimate truth, and that Islam has been made so easy for everybody that in reality there are no laws and we just conform with whatever the values of our times are. There has to be that healthy balance and middle ground.

And so my philosophy throughout all of these lectures has been that where there is room for change, where there is leeway, and culture and society are forcing us to rethink through the tradition, the paradigm that we follow — the traditionalist paradigm — allows us to rethink through the tradition. No problem, we should do so. However, where we have an explicit, authoritative text from Allah, or a hadith that needs to be applied in the situation we are dealing with — or unanimous consensus, which of course is the most definitive, because Qur'an and hadith can be interpreted depending on how you look at them, but unanimous consensus is not interpreted, it is unanimous consensus. By that I mean that with a verse from the Qur'an or a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, so many times scholars will look at the same thing and derive different interpretations. But when you have unanimous consensus, well, then that solves the issue.

So the bottom line, what I'm trying to say, is that I do not consider myself to be a cut-and-paste literalist or fundamentalist — and I don't think anybody who listens to my lectures actually accuses me of that. I'm saying this because where there is room for change, I will be the first to advocate that change, if you listen to so many other Q&As that I've given. And where the texts are definitive, where the texts are clear-cut, well, then there has to be "We hear and we obey."

Also, another disclaimer, because again we live in times where no matter what you say, somebody's going to pick on it and read in. Obviously I'm speaking from a spiritual or a religious paradigm. I'm not speaking from the legal paradigm of the lands that we are living in. Obviously, in Western lands, once a woman comes of age, a man comes of age, they are technically free to do whatever they want according to the laws of the land. So what I'm saying is not enforceable on anybody living in these lands. You're simply asking religious advice; you're asking about the spiritual realities. And therefore I am telling you: this is the response based upon the relationship between you and your Lord. You can choose to take it, you can choose to reject it; that is up to you. At the end of the day, these Western lands that we live in obviously have ultimate freedom to do as you please when it comes to marriage. And therefore this is simply advice that is being given from a spiritual perspective, and what you do beyond this is up to you. If a person chooses to take another path, that is their prerogative in this land, and then they have to answer to Allah on the Day of Judgment.

One other caveat before I get to the actual fiqh, and this is very important. Brothers and sisters, when we talk about Islamic law, when we talk about Shari'ah, when we talk about fiqh, we need to separate the wisdom of the ruling from the legal cause of the ruling. This is one of the most common mistakes that the average Muslim falls into when they look at Islamic law. The wisdom — in Arabic, hikmah — is a general reason: we can say that because of this reason such a ruling has come down from Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. So the wisdom, we can say, is: it seems this is why Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala legislated a particular ruling.

However, the wisdom of a particular ruling is not the cause of the ruling, because it is possible for the wisdom to exist and it is possible for the wisdom to not exist. The legal ruling will only be applied when the cause of the ruling — in Arabic this is called 'illah — when the 'illah of the ruling exists. When there is the 'illah, when there is the cause, the ruling will exist. We would expect that the wisdom and the 'illah and the ruling are all simultaneous. We would expect this to be the default, and it is the default. However, if in a particular scenario the wisdom of the ruling is not manifested, the ruling still applies. I hope that is clear, and I'll give you a number of examples so we understand.

A simple example is that of shortening the prayer: to pray Dhuhr, which is four, as two rak'ahs. The 'illah is travel. The wisdom is to make life easier. It was difficult to travel at that time, to get off the caravan, to combine the prayers, to pray two. So the wisdom is the ease of the travel; the actual cause is the travel itself. Now suppose somebody were to argue, "Hey, in those days they couldn't just stop the caravan and pray four. These days we're just driving a car." Or, "In those days they didn't have air conditioning, and these days we have full air conditioning, we're in the plane — why should we worry about this four and two? Everything is so easy now." We're going to say that the wisdom of the ruling was to make it easier.

Fasting, for example: the issue of not fasting when traveling. They would say the wisdom is to make the fast easier for the person, because it's so difficult to walk when you're fasting; it's so difficult to be traveling when you're fasting. If somebody were to say, "Hey guys, today we have the airplane, and you're just sitting there with cool air conditioning flowing, and you don't have to move a finger, you're going 500 miles an hour; therefore we're going to say that you are not allowed to break your fast when you're traveling, because the wisdom doesn't exist" — the response is no. The ruling comes as a result of its legal cause, the 'illah, which is travel, and it does not come as a result of the wisdom. In case the wisdom does not exist, the ruling will still exist.

Now why do I say this? Because we're going to come to this notion of protecting the sanctity of the woman, protecting the honor of the woman. We're going to come to this notion of making sure that nobody takes advantage of the lady. This is a wisdom; it is not the cause. It is a wisdom. If somebody were to say, "Hey, I am more knowledgeable than my wali," if somebody were to say, "My wali doesn't know anything, and I am a better person to judge," we will say — and we're going to come to this; it doesn't mean this is the end of the story — that the default ruling does not change, because what you're referring to is a wisdom, that the protection needs to be done. And the default ruling is not based on the wisdom; it is based on what we call the 'illah, or the legal cause.

And by the way, the same applies in secular law as well. Let me give you a simple example that will help illustrate this point from a secular paradigm: the speed limits. You're driving on the highway, and there's a limit of 70 miles an hour. Now, why? What is the wisdom of that ruling? The wisdom of that ruling is to protect life. The wisdom of that ruling is to avoid drastic, tragic accidents. The wisdom of that ruling is that nobody should be going at 100 miles an hour, because that is fatal, that is lethal; you're going to kill yourself or kill other people. And so you should go at a reasonable pace, so that even if, God forbid, an accident happens, you minimize the damage. That is the wisdom.

Now, let me ask you an honest question: does everybody have the same level of driving skills? What if somebody would argue — and maybe they're correct — "Hey, I'm a speed race driver, that's my profession, and I can drive 90 miles an hour just as safely as I can drive 60 miles an hour"? In fact, there is no doubt that there are some people who are safer drivers at 90 miles an hour than others that are driving at 60 miles an hour. Isn't that the case? For some people, those rules don't make sense: why would you restrict this expert to 70 miles an hour? Actually, that expert should go 80, 90, 100, and they know exactly when to speed, when to brake; they have a fancy car with good brakes, whatever. Whereas other people — for whatever reason, impediments, impairments, whatever — in fact should not even be given 70; they should be given 50. In fact, how many of us think that certain people should not even be driving when we see them on the highway?

Khayr, the point is that this is a good illustration. What if this person who's speeding at 90 is caught by the police, and he goes to the court and says to the judge, "Hey, I am qualified. That rule doesn't apply to me, because I'm smarter than everybody else"? What do you think the judge is going to say? Similarly, the Shari'ah has come with generic laws. Generally speaking, those laws are for the benefit of society. It is very possible that in an individual case we don't see the wisdom of that law — it's very possible; we don't see the wisdom manifested. It does not change the default ruling. That's something we have to be very clear about, because we always get this issue of, "Hey, but what about this, or what about that?" Islamic law is not based upon "what about this and what about that." Islamic law is based upon the legal cause, what is called the 'illah. And so in case the wisdom is not manifested in a particular situation, it will not change the legal ruling — even though other mechanisms can be done, as we have said.

Now, by the way, all of this preliminary discussion was done because all too often, I think, scholars just jump in to quote the evidence: "Imam al-Shafi'i said this, and the hadith says that," and this and that. And we need to understand that a lot of our young men and women, and especially our young women who are about to get married, really are struggling to understand the wisdoms of some of these laws. And I sympathize with that struggle.

But we do need to take a step back and point out that for pretty much all of human history before this one generation that we just happened to be born in, for pretty much the entirety of the human race, marriage and gender and the roles of gender were looked at in a very, very different light. All that we're seeing now of this individualism — "me, myself and I," and "what I want to do," and "my life" — all of this is very, very recent. And even in these lands that we live in, we can date this quite literally to the late 60s and early 70s. This is when it all began. So even though society is changing — I understand the world is no longer the way that it used to be — we do need to point out that that is a relatively modern change. And frankly, not for this question but in other questions and other lectures, we do need to get into the effects that these changes have had: the detrimental effects on family, on society, on sexuality, what is happening to the world around us internally and externally. All of this goes back to a number of key changes that took place in this time frame. Anyway, all of this is separate to the point here.

So to summarize all of this, as a conclusion before we get to the fiqh: we need to understand the difference between wisdom and cause. Just in case the wisdom doesn't exist, the cause will still bring about the ruling. We also need to understand that Islamic law does allow for some change, but not unconditional change. So what I'm trying to point out is that, inshallah, I consider myself to be of those who are pushing for change where change is allowed. Therefore, when no change is allowed and I say that no change is allowed, understand that I'm not coming from a literalist or a fundamentalist paradigm. I'm trying my best to work within the situation as we can.

And then the third point that I mentioned is the cultural realities that we live in. As we go through these issues, let us be brave enough to problematize modernity. Let us be brave enough to problematize our own modern culture and not just accept it to be the ethical default. It might be the political default; it doesn't mean it is the ethical norm. And we need to be brave enough to challenge our presumptions and to challenge the notions that we've absorbed from the time and the place that we have lived in.

With all of that, let us now get to what Islamic law says, and what the main opinions are about having a wali for marriage.

So the first position in this regard is the position of the vast majority of the scholars of Islam, and the position of all of the schools of Islamic law except for one. This includes the Malikis and the Shafi'is and the Hanbalis and the Zahiris, and pretty much every other major scholar that has come, except for one primary, fundamental school, which is the Hanafi school — that's the exception. The majority of scholars past and present, classical, pre-modern and modern, and the majority of Islamic schools have said that the nikah, the marriage contract, will not be valid without a wali. If there is no wali, then there is no marriage. The marriage contract cannot and does not take place between the bride and the groom; rather, it takes place between the groom and the wali, with the consent of the bride.

So this is the position of pretty much all of the schools of Islamic law except for one: that the wali is a necessary prerequisite, a necessary condition. It is called the rukn, basically; it's a necessary part and parcel. There is no contract, you cannot have a marriage, there is no nikah without the approval of the wali, we can say — whether the wali himself is present or delegates somebody. But the point is the wali has to approve, and then the nikah will take place. Of course, this is the wali from the bride's side; Islamic law does not require the wali from the groom's side.

And once again, this is one of those cultural issues that comes up: why not? This is a longer discussion, but it is very, very correct to point out that while Islamic law views the genders as being spiritually equal in the eyes of Allah, Islamic law does have differences between the roles and the responsibilities of the two genders. That is an undeniable fact. And the only way out of this, frankly, is to completely reject normative Islamic law, to completely reject the basic tenets of the Qur'an and Sunnah, and to redevelop something completely obscure and unknown — which then comes to the point of how much you are going to change the religion, and at what point that much change makes the religion not the religion of Islam anymore. All of these are questions that need to be discussed by those who are going to go to that level. From our perspective, we're not going to go down there today. We're simply going to say that, according to that position, the wali is a necessary requirement, a part and parcel of the nikah contract.

Now, this is position number one. Within this position we can subcategorize into two, 1A and 1B, and then there's position two. So there are two major positions, and within the first we'll have 1A and 1B.

1A: that the wali always has the right of veto, and the wali's approval must always be sought, regardless of the circumstances of the lady — whether she's previously unmarried, or whether she has been married and then divorced and wants to remarry, or widowed and wants to remarry. In all circumstances, this group of scholars and 'ulama would argue that the wali's approval must be sought, and that if for whatever reason the wali does not agree, then the nikah cannot take place — unless (and we're going to come to this) the lady appeals to a higher authority, the court or whatnot, and the wali is taken away and another wali is put in his place. But the woman cannot, of herself, go ahead and perform the contract. This would be 1A: the wali does have veto power in all circumstances, whether the woman has been unmarried or whether the woman has been previously married.

1B is that the wali is still required. However, the wilayah, or the wali, of the lady who has been previously divorced or has been widowed essentially becomes a token wali. If there is a clash between the divorced lady who wants to remarry, or the widowed lady who wants to marry, and her wali — meaning obviously the only lady left is the unmarried lady, the lady who has never been married, right? — if there is a clash between the divorcee or the widow and her wali, she has the right, without going to a third party, to strip his wilayah away and give it to somebody else: go to another cousin, go to an uncle, go to somebody and say, "You will be my wali for the marriage." She does not need the permission of a particular wali. She needs a wali.

By the way, both of these still have a wali. The difference, though, is in the power of the wali. In 1A, the wali always outranks the lady. 1B is that the wali outranks the lady in power when she has been previously unmarried — it's her first marriage. And 1B would say that if she has been married, and then for whatever reason — divorce or the death of the husband — she now wants to remarry, in this case she has the right to basically marry whomever she pleases. And in case her primary wali says no, she has the right to say, "Well, okay, I'll choose another wali," and she then chooses an uncle or a cousin, and then the marriage will take place. And this, let's call it 1B.

And the technical terms for this are wali al-mujbir and wali al-musharik. Wali al-mujbir is the one that has the right to veto; that's 1A. Wali al-musharik is the one that is just taking part in the ceremony.

And the position that I'm advocating in this Q&A is 1B. This is the position that I personally follow when I have cases in front of me, and it is the position that I think does make the most sense — even though, again, with respect to 1A and position 2, I have the utmost respect for all of those scholars. But obviously every one of us who has to deal with cases has to have a position. So my position, the default, the one that I'm advocating and the one that I have been advocating throughout my Q&As, is basically 1B: **the unmarried lady requires her wali's permission, and that permission has veto status, whereas the previously married lady gets the wali, but the wali becomes a technicality.** The wali becomes just any wali that is her close relative that can count as a wali, and she then performs the marriage even if the primary wali says no. It's her business; she has to face the consequences of that in this world. Obviously, there's no sin on her for doing that.

That's position 1B, and that is the position of many 'ulama past and present. It's a classical position, nothing new; it's very well known and standard that the unmarried lady requires the permission of her wali, whereas the lady who was married and then divorced, and the widowed lady, has more right concerning her life and her business than her wali does.

So that's 1A and 1B. The second opinion is, of course, the famous position of the Hanafi school, and the position that has been attributed to a number of tabi'un, including al-Zuhri, and it has also been narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri: that they allowed a woman to get married without her wali's approval. And even if her wali said no, they said she can still get married. And this is an opinion. Nobody can deny the veracity of the opinion, that it exists. It is an opinion that has been held by one of the major and most vibrant schools of Islamic law, and it is a position that therefore cannot just be dismissed.

However, as I will argue in this lecture, the majority position really does have so many evidences that I cannot just find leeway and dismiss it and choose the position of the other school — with respect, with the utmost respect to the other school. And of course, anybody who is a follower of that school, you have the right to follow your Islamic law. Nobody's telling you that you should leave that. However, anybody who is by default following any of the other schools should definitely not just pick and choose another one because of convenience.

Now, what are some of the evidences that are used by the majority opinion, those who say that a wali is required? There are so many evidences that we're going to have to summarize them. One of the most common evidences is an entire series of Qur'anic verses pertaining to marriage where, pretty much by default, most of the time that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala references marriage, when He talks about women marrying, He uses a different verb. That verb is ankaha, and ankaha means to get married off. He doesn't use the word nakaha, and nakaha means that you marry. So Allah switches verbs — it's transitive versus intransitive — who's doing it. When Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is talking about ladies getting married, He is addressing the awliya, the wali, and He is saying to the wali, "Do not get your ladies married off," or "Get your ladies married off." So the addressee is the wali. It is as if the wali is the one making the decision, or at least enforcing the decision after the lady says she wants it or not; the wali is the one who is doing the contract and taking care of the contract on behalf of the lady.

So the Qur'an has so many verses in this genre. For example, Surah al-Baqarah, verse 221: Allah speaks to the men, and Allah says, do not do nikah — He's speaking to the men — do not do nikah with pagan ladies, those who worship idols, until they believe in Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Then when it comes to women, it's a different verb, if you know your Arabic, and that verb is: do not marry off your women to men who are worshipping idols. Notice the difference in the tenses. When Allah is talking about the man getting married, Allah says, "You men, do not get married to ladies who are practicing idolatry." Then when Allah talks about Muslim ladies, He says, "And do not, O men, get your daughters" — or the people that you're in charge of; He's speaking to the awliya — "do not get your ladies married off." So now Allah is speaking to the one who has the right to veto, and that is the wali.

Also in the Qur'an: "Get married off" — again the transitive verb — that you're not doing the marriage, but your ladies that are under your control, have them married off. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says, "Marry them with the permission of their families." Now, these two verses are not technically fully in the context of what we're talking about, because they deal with the right hand — ama and milk al-yamin. Nonetheless, the concept is there that the permission must be given by those in authority.

And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala mentions in Surah al-Qasas the story of Musa and his father-in-law-to-be, when he went to Madyan. Allah says in the Qur'an that the father-in-law-to-be of Musa said — the father says to Musa — "I want to offer you one of my two daughters in marriage." Once again, the father is the one saying, "I shall marry my daughter off to you." So all of these verses indicate very clearly that the one who is doing the technicalities of the nikah, the one who is deciding whether it's going to take place or not, the one who has the veto power, is the wali.

And perhaps one of the most explicit verses in this regard is also in Surah al-Baqarah, in the same series where Allah mentions nikah and talaq. Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says that when you divorce women and they finish their divorced time frame — they finish their waiting period — then do not prevent them from remarrying, or from marrying whoever they want to, if they choose to do so with ma'ruf, in a good manner.

Now, this verse was revealed because of an incident in Medina. It is an authentic hadith reported in multiple books of hadith, including in Sahih Bukhari, that Ma'qil ibn Yasar married his sister off to their cousin, and some fighting happened between the couple, and the cousin ends up divorcing the sister and sends her back to the house of Ma'qil. And Ma'qil loses his temper, gets angry at his brother-in-law-slash-cousin, and basically they're falling out. Then the 'iddah finishes, and she is now a free lady, the sister of Ma'qil. The husband comes back apologizing, wanting to make up. He speaks to his ex-wife, and they agree to give it another chance. They agree that they're going to make it work out this time, and she agrees to marry her cousin; she wants to get remarried again. And Ma'qil ibn Yasar said, "No, wallahi, I will never do this. I welcomed you into our household as a brother-in-law. I gave you my sister. I did this and that. And then you mistreated her and sent her back."

Now here we have the classic, the classic issue, right? This clash: his sister wants to marry, and her brother — the parents were not in the picture — her brother is saying, "No, you're not going to marry; this man has dishonored us by divorcing you." And so Allah revealed in the Qur'an, "fala ta'duluhunna." The addressee is Ma'qil: O Ma'qil, do not stop, do not act as a barrier between your sister and the man that she wants to marry. It's not your responsibility now to act as that barrier.

Now, what is the evidence here? The evidence is that the very fact that Allah had to reveal that you cannot stop this marriage, the very fact that Allah is addressing him, indicates that he had some power. And now the question arises: how much power? Did he have veto power? Or — which is what I'm arguing — he didn't have that veto power anymore, but he still had a wali status. And Allah is saying, now that she is fully capable of making that decision, you cannot come between her and her decision. That is the argument that I'm making.

Other scholars, by the way... and I'm not going to go down the controversy over 1A and 1B and the evidences; that's maybe for another Q&A. In this Q&A we're not going to go down there. I do realize, by the way, that there are strong evidences on both sides. I'm not dismissing 1A at all. But I'm simply saying, again, for me and the position that I follow, 1B is very clear-cut, to me at least. And there are a number of traditions that I see to be very self-evident that the divorced lady has the ultimate right to make her decision, even if her wali says no.

Now, these are the Qur'anic evidences. There are many hadith as well in this regard — many. Of them, the most famous hadith is the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: "La nikaha illa bi-wali" — there is no nikah except with a wali. So again, this is a negation: there is no nikah except with a wali. This hadith is reported in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah and al-Hakim and the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, and a number of other books as well.

And the problem comes — and this is the whole issue here — that all of the ahadith that are explicit are not in Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. They're in the other books, books lesser than that. And the ahadith that are implicit, and in Bukhari and Muslim, are not as explicit as what we need for this issue. That's why the Hanafi school is able to... as we will come to.

So this hadith, "La nikaha illa bi-wali": al-Tirmidhi himself says that there's some controversy over whether it is a continuous chain or a broken chain, and then he prefers that it is a continuous chain, so he says it is authentic. But there is a controversy over whether it is an authentic hadith or not, from the time of Tirmidhi up until our times.

And the hadith in Tirmidhi as well — three times — that whichever lady marries herself off without her wali, her marriage is batil, her marriage is invalid, her marriage is invalid. And if they differ over who's going to be the wali, or there's no wali, then the Sultan will be the wali — the leader or the community will be the wali for the one who has no wali. And this hadith as well is subject to some controversy.

In the Sunan of Abu Dawud we have the hadith that the wali has no affair with the previously married lady, the widow or the divorcee; the wali does not have control over her. And as for the yatimah — and the yatimah here literally means the orphan, but it also means the young girl; sometimes you call the young girl that — the young girl is asked whether she wants to marry or not, and if she is quiet, then her quietness, her silence, is considered to be her acceptance. So once again we have the notion of the wali being involved and taking charge and getting permission from the lady, but once that is done, then he is the one doing the nikah.

Also in Sahih Muslim we have the hadith: the lady that has been married... Now again, I'm translating this as "the lady that has been married." Realize that even how you translate these goes back to whether you prefer 1A or 1B. Because I prefer 1B, I'm doing a different translation. Those who prefer 1A have a different understanding of this hadith, but for now we'll leave that controversy between 1A and 1B. The ayyim — and I'm translating the ayyim here as the one who has already been married — has more right concerning herself than her wali. And the one who has not been married before, the unmarried lady, must be asked permission. And this is in Sahih Muslim. Now, that's in Sahih Muslim, but it doesn't mention that the nikah must have the wali. The concept is indirect, but it is not direct. And in Sahih Bukhari as well there is a similar hadith in this regard.

Now, these are the evidences of the primary school. The crux of their evidence really is that the Qur'an seems to address the wali, and there are a number of hadith that mention there is no nikah without a wali, and put together, these are authentic hadith.

How do the Hanafis respond to this? The Hanafis say that, well, the Qur'an doesn't always address the wali. The Hanafis do not deny that it is better to have a wali; the Hanafis simply say it's not a necessary requirement. And in case there is no wali, they say, or the wali for whatever reason is not there, the woman may herself get married and act on her own behalf. She does not need a wali, and she can do her own marriage without any wali, even if she is previously unmarried. If it's her first marriage, she can act on her own behalf.

Now, a footnote here: even the Hanafis amongst themselves have like five or six opinions with minor differences, but this is the mainstream position. What I'm telling you is like the default — and this is reported from Imam Abu Hanifa and Muhammad al-Hasan and Abu Yusuf — the default of the Hanafi madhhab, and you can look this up in Ibn al-Humam and other famous books of the Hanafi school of law. The default of their madhhab is that the young lady, previously unmarried, may marry herself off as long as her husband-to-be is of a similar background — meaning he is somebody who's appropriate for her — and somebody who gives her her mahr that is equivalent to her status.

Now again, even these scholars said that the groom must be suitable. Now, who gets to define what is suitable, right? Because what they were worried about is an unmarried lady being taken advantage of. And so even they put that in: somebody from the same socioeconomic and, in those times, cultural background.

Because again, this is another point of the backlash that I got: that culture is no longer important. And I understand this is an ongoing conversation. Culture was very important for most of human history. These days, I understand that culture is secondary, and I'm not arguing that culture is definitive. I'm not arguing that at all. But do understand that for most of human history, it was very important that the husband and wife be of a similar background — socioeconomically, intellectually, culturally. They thought the marriage would get along better, and it would not work out otherwise. That's the way that they felt. The world that we live in is a very different world, and I'm willing to acknowledge that that is not a requirement anymore; the Shari'ah does not come and mandate that a person has to be of the same culture. I never said that. But I did say that generally speaking — generally speaking — birds of a feather flock together. I think that's a general rule. But of course there are many exceptions, and that's not Shari'ah; that's just normative human history.

Nonetheless, the Hanafis say that if the groom is suitable for the lady and gives her the mahr that other ladies of her socioeconomic status would get, then the nikah is valid even if there's no wali, and she can be the wali herself.

Now, what is their evidence for this? They say that, firstly, there are at least one or two verses where Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala seems to indicate that the woman has the right over her marriage, and it's not talking to the wali. Of them is Surah al-Baqarah, verse 234: that there is no sin on you in whatever they decide to do in a way that is honorable and respectful — "whatever they," meaning the women here. So Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is literally saying that she has the right. Now, the response by the majority is that the reference here is that she may choose to marry and she may choose to remain single, and it doesn't mean that the wali has no role. It simply means that she now has the opportunity to basically give the message out that she's looking for a groom and she's interested in marriage, or she cannot do that. So the point is they have a way of interpreting that, and it's not the way that the Hanafis understand it.

The other issue that the Hanafis bring is that all of these hadith that we brought forth — "There is no nikah without a wali," "Whoever marries without a wali, their nikah is batil, batil, batil" — the Hanafis say, according to their understanding, these hadith are not authentic. So they simply point out — and it is correct to point out — that certain scholars criticize these hadith, and so, generally speaking, they put these hadith to the side.

And they also then bring up another issue, which is a bit more technical, and that is that they believe that if the narrator of the hadith himself does something against the hadith, this shows that the hadith is somehow not authentic. And so they point out that Aisha radiyallahu 'anha, who is narrating one of these hadith, apparently herself got one of her nieces married without her brother's approval.

And the story goes as follows. Aisha radiyallahu 'anha of course had a younger brother by the name of Abdul Rahman ibn Abi Bakr. Abdul Rahman was her younger brother — remember the famous hadith of the Hajj, that Abdul Rahman was the one who, from Masjid Aisha, from Tan'im, took her and then brought her to the tawaf and sa'i one more time. So Abdul Rahman had a daughter by the name of Hafsa. Abdul Rahman was away on a long journey, and in that interim period — this is of course after the death of the Prophet ﷺ — Aisha radiyallahu 'anha got her niece Hafsa married to al-Mundhir ibn Zubayr, the younger brother of Abdullah ibn Zubayr. The famous Abdullah ibn Zubayr had a younger brother called al-Mundhir ibn Zubayr. And so Aisha got her niece married to al-Mundhir while her brother was not in the picture. Her brother was away — that's her wali, Hafsa's wali.

And when her brother returned, he was very angry, and he said, "How could this happen? How could you do this when I'm not here?" Obviously, understandably, he was very hurt. And so the issue was then brought back to al-Mundhir, the groom, and al-Mundhir said, "I will leave the affair to the father. If he wants to cancel, then I will cancel." And the father then said, "No, khalas, now that it's happened, let it be." And so the marriage did in fact go ahead — meaning the marriage had already taken place, but the marriage was then allowed to continue.

So the fact that Aisha radiyallahu 'anha got her niece married in the absence of her brother is an indication, according to the Hanafis, that she did not view the wilayah to be necessary.

The response to this is a bit more complicated. The response is, firstly, they say the action of a companion does not take precedence over the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ. This is what the majority say. And so even if the companion does something, the hadith has a higher authority over it. Secondly, they'll point out that Aisha did not act as a wali; rather, she had another male relative act as a wali in this nikah. What she did was she kind of sort of took Abdul Rahman out of the picture and did not ask his permission, and got her niece married off. And the actual wali — there was a wali involved, but it wasn't the father; it was another relative. I don't know who it was; actually, the books don't mention who it was. But another relative, a brother, an uncle, whatever — couldn't have been an uncle, excuse me — but another person got involved, and he acted as the wali. So it's not as if she became the wali; rather, she did a reorientation of the wali. She took the wilayah of the father away, which irritated the father immensely, and she gave it to somebody else. So that is the way that we understand this.

And then also, by the way, it needs to be said here: hey, firstly, this is Aisha. It's not just anybody. And this is her niece; it's not just a stranger. And this is a girl that she's raised, and her younger brother and she might have a relationship we don't know about. And by the way, the groom was very noble, coming from a very well-known family, the family of Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam. I mean, what more do you want? And so maybe Aisha assumed that this is a golden opportunity to have this marriage take place, and that the father would approve. The point is, there are a million scenarios of why, what if, why. And we should simply understand that the hadith in this case will have precedence and priority over the actions of a very respected companion, and of course the wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

The Hanafis, by the way, also mention a logical reasoning, and they say that just like the lady does not need to ask permission when she spends her money, why would she need to ask permission when she gets married? And of course that logic and reasoning appeals immensely to many people in our times. The response goes that, firstly, marriage is not just a simple one-off, like you buy a purse or something of this nature. It is a lifelong commitment. Secondly, it has repercussions beyond you yourself; there are family repercussions. And then thirdly, we are not the ones putting these conditions. The hadith is coming and saying the nikah has to have a wali. If this hadith did not exist, this logic would be very sound: why should she need permission? We are not putting the permission; the permission is being put by the hadith itself, that she needs to get the permission of her wali.

So all of this being said, I understand that the Hanafi position is very appealing to many of our younger brothers and sisters. If they happen to follow the Hanafi madhhab and they take recourse to this action, what can be done? It is a valid position, and if it is their school of law, it is their school of law. However, I do consider the other position to be the stronger one, because of the number of evidences, the explicit nature of the evidences, and the explicit hadith in this regard. The hadith are authentic, by the way; the vast majority of scholars of hadith have considered them so, because it's not just one hadith. There are at least seven hadith — at least seven different hadith — about the concept that the nikah has to have a wali. I quoted you the top two or three of them, but there are more that I did not quote you.

The issue also comes, before we get to some advice, in case there's a clash about the order of the walis. What if the father is not in the picture — he's passed away — what happens then? And again, the order is a much easier issue. According to the Hanbali school of law, you start with the father, and then you go upward: so the grandfather, if he's still alive. Then if there is no ascendant, you go to the descendant. So suppose she's getting married and she has a teenage son; then the son becomes the wali of the divorced or the widowed mother, and then the grandson or whatnot. Suppose there are no sons; then in this case her full brother, then her brother from her father's side if there's a half sibling, after that her full uncle, and then her half uncle, and then her full cousin from her uncle. "Uncle" here is of course the paternal uncle, so it is the father's brother; and then if there's no uncle, the father's brother's sons become her wali. So basically the Hanbali madhhab is leaning towards — and this is the majority position — the father's side, because the father is the wali, so his relatives would come. Generally speaking, most of the schools of law do not consider the wilayah to go to the mother's side for the unmarried lady.

Now suppose there is no relative from the father's side. What is to be done in this case? If you live in an Islamic land, the Islamic court will appoint a wali for you. And if you live in a non-Muslim land, you should go to the masjid, and the imam will then either act himself or appoint a wali for you, and that would be your wali. Not a problem in that case.

Also, by the way, one point that should be mentioned here is the concept of wakalah, of tawkil, of the wali. It's very common that a distant wali in terms of blood might be closer to the family proximity-wise and relationship-wise — like you have a better relationship — than a closer wali in terms of blood. So let me give you a classic example. Most of us are living in the West. We might have an uncle living back home, and we have a cousin — a father's brother's son, for example — living in a different state. And because we're in this country, we're closer to that cousin than we are to the distant uncle. In this case, all that needs to be done is that the wali who is distant by physical proximity simply says, "Okay, I give my permission to the cousin; you can stand in my place, no problem." So this is handing the wali over.

By the way, this can be done in any situation or circumstance. For example, if the father cannot physically be present — suppose the father is overseas and the lady is in a different land — the father can say to somebody in the community that is there, he can call up and say, "Okay, so-and-so, you're my friend, I know you; you become the wali for my daughter." So the father then delegates. This is called a delegation, or a wakalah. It can be done for any reason; you don't have to have a medical need. It can be done for any reason: the wali can hand over, can delegate the responsibility to somebody else.

Okay, so before we get to the advice in case of controversy, the conclusion of the fiqh aspect is that **it is very clear from the Qur'an and Sunnah that the nikah takes place with a wali.** And even if the lady is previously divorced or widowed, there must be a nominal wali. So the wali is still there, but in that case she has more right than her wali does, and nobody can veto her if she decides to do so. This is the position that I'm advocating, which is 1B.
